title: Multi-Level Marketing Businesses and Pyramid Schemes
summary: FTC consumer guide on how MLMs work, how to spot a pyramid scheme, and the costs and questions to weigh before joining.

assertions.quote: Most people who join legitimate MLMs make little or no money. Some of them lose money.
Your income would be based mostly on how many people you recruit, not how much product you sell.

verdicts.note: This is the legal definition regulators use to distinguish pyramid schemes from MLMs.

AARP's consumer guidance lists a focus on recruiting rather than selling, with retail sales unrelated to rewards, as the sign an MLM may be a pyramid scheme; a definitional statement rather than evidence.
In every one of the 350 MLM compensation plans Taylor analysed, rewards were paid primarily for aggressively recruiting a large downline rather than for retailing products to outside customers.

assertions.quote: Even if the start-up costs seem low, additional expenses can add up quickly.

verdicts.note: Expense-adjusted earnings analyses of MLMs find most participants net negative.

assertions.quote: Promoters make extravagant promises about your earning potential. Stop. These promises are false.
If you need to borrow money or use your credit card to finance your expenses, you may face hefty interest charges too.
